definition: Wells that produce a mixture of oil and gas are labeled 'gas well' or 'oil well' based on the ratio of gas volume produced to oil volume produced, using a conventional threshold of 100,000 cubic feet of gas per barrel of oil.
core_idea: Because virtually all wells produce some mixture of both oil and gas, the gas-to-oil ratio (GOR) is used as a naming convention rather than a strict physical category: below the threshold the well is called an oil well, above it a gas well.
key_points: Gas-oil ratio = volume of natural gas produced (ft3) divided by volume of crude oil produced (BBL) over a given period.
Oil well: gas-oil ratio less than 100,000 ft3/BBL.
Gas well: gas-oil ratio greater than 100,000 ft3/BBL.
All wells generally produce both gas and oil in some proportion; the label just reflects which dominates.
relationships: Applies to output from traditional wells described in the surrounding text.
trading_implications: GOR labeling affects how a well's output is categorized for market/production reporting purposes, even though actual output is mixed.
caveats: A 'gas well' or 'oil well' label does not mean the well produces only one fuel type — it reflects a ratio threshold, not exclusivity.

variables.Gas produced: cubic feet (ft3) of natural gas produced over a period
variables.Oil produced: barrels (BBL) of crude oil produced over the same period
variables.100,000 ft3/BBL: conventional dividing line between classifying a well as oil vs. gas
